arithmetic operators: Symbols (+, -, *, /, %) that perform math on numeric values, with type promotion applied to mixed operands.
compound assignment: Operators like +=, -=, *=, /=, %= that combine an operation with assignment to update a variable in place.
increment/decrement: The ++ and -- operators that add or subtract one; prefix changes the value before use, postfix after.
integer division truncates: Dividing two integers in Java discards the fractional part, so 7/2 yields 3 rather than 3.5.
literal syntax: The fixed notation for constant values, where 1, 1.0, true, and 'a' denote different data types.
loss of information in narrowing cast: Converting a wider type to a narrower one drops data, as casting 3.9 to int gives 3.
operator precedence: The order in which operations evaluate; *, /, % bind tighter than +, -, and equal precedence runs left to right.
widening: An automatic conversion from a smaller numeric type to a larger one, such as int to double, without a cast.
autoboxing: Java's automatic conversion between a primitive type and its corresponding wrapper object, such as int and Integer.
integer methods: Static members of the Integer class, such as Integer.parseInt() and Integer.MAX_VALUE.
key methods: Common String operations including length(), substring(a,b), indexOf(), equals(), and compareTo().
null reference: A reference that points to no object; calling a method on it throws a NullPointerException.
static methods: Methods invoked on the class itself rather than on an instance of the class.
string is immutable: A String cannot be changed; its methods return new String objects instead of modifying the original.
de morgan's laws: Logical rules stating that !(A&&B) equals !A||!B, swapping && and || when negation is distributed.
equivalent boolean expressions: Different boolean expressions that always produce the same result, often simplified using De Morgan's laws.
mutual exclusion in if-else chains: In an if-else if chain, only the first true condition runs and later branches are skipped.
nested if vs. if-else if: Nested ifs each evaluate independently, while an if-else if chain selects only one branch to execute.
accumulator pattern: A loop technique that builds a running total or result by repeatedly adding to a variable.
count pattern: A loop technique that increments a counter each time a condition is met to tally occurrences.
init; condition; update: The three parts of a for loop header: initialize a variable, test a condition, then update each iteration.
iterating: Looping through items in sequence, such as visiting each character of a string with charAt in a for loop.
nested for loops: A for loop inside another, where total iterations equal the outer count times the inner count.
off-by-one errors: Common loop mistakes caused by confusing < with <= and running one too many or too few times.
output patterns from nested loops: Visual structures like triangles, grids, and tables produced by nested loops printing rows and columns.
search pattern: A loop technique using a boolean flag set to true once the target item is found.
string indexing: Accessing characters by position, where valid indexes run from 0 to length()-1.
time complexity of nested loops: The growth rate of nested loops; two loops over n items run in O(n squared) time.
calling static: Invoking a static method through the class name (ClassName.method()) rather than through an object.
method overloading: Defining multiple methods with the same name but different parameter lists in the same class.
methods: Named blocks of code in a class, including accessors (getters), mutators (setters), and other operations.
private fields, public methods: The standard encapsulation pattern that hides data fields and exposes controlled access through public methods.
this keyword: A reference to the current object, used to distinguish instance variables from parameters of the same name.
when to use static: Static is appropriate for utility methods and class-level constants or counters shared across instances.
why encapsulation is beneficial: Encapsulation protects an object from entering an invalid state by controlling access to its data.
array as a parameter vs. primitive param: An array parameter shares a reference so changes are visible to the caller, while a primitive is copied.
arrays are reference types: Arrays are passed by reference, so modifications made inside a method affect the original array.
default values: Newly allocated array elements are filled with type defaults: 0, 0.0, false, or null.
for-each loop for read-only traversal: An enhanced for loop (for(int x : arr)) that reads each element in turn without modifying the array.
off-by-one: An indexing error; the last valid index of an array is its length minus one.
selection sort and insertion sort: Two simple comparison sorting algorithms, both running in O(n squared) time.
sequential search: Checking elements one by one in O(n) time, unlike binary search which is O(log n) but needs a sorted array.
arraylist methods: Core ArrayList operations: add, get, set, remove, and size for adding, reading, changing, deleting, and counting.
arraylist stores objects, not primitives: An ArrayList holds objects, so primitives must use wrapper classes like Integer rather than int.
e: In list.add(e) the element is appended to the end; add(i,e) inserts at index i and remove(i) deletes at index i.
removing elements while iterating with i: To delete safely during indexed iteration, traverse backward or adjust the index after each removal.
access: A grid cell is reached with grid[row][col]; grid.length gives the row count and grid[0].length the column count.
column-major traversal: Visiting a 2D array with the outer loop over columns and the inner loop over rows.
diagonal traversal: Visiting the cells where the row index equals the column index, such as grid[i][i].
jagged arrays: Two-dimensional arrays whose rows may have different lengths.
row-major traversal: Visiting a 2D array with the outer loop over rows and the inner loop over columns.
has-a relationship: A composition relationship where one object contains another, such as a Car having an Engine.
is-a relationship: An inheritance relationship where a subclass is a kind of its superclass, such as a Dog being an Animal.
head-and-tail recursion patterns: A recursive approach that processes the first element and recurses on the rest of the data.
order of operations: In recursion, the recursive call executes before the calling frame returns and completes its work.
recursive array processing: Solving array tasks recursively, such as computing a sum, searching, or finding the min or max.
recursive string operations: Solving string tasks recursively, such as reversing, checking palindromes, or substring search.
stack frames: Each method call adds a frame to the call stack, which unwinds as calls return.
when recursion is natural: Recursion fits problems like tree traversal, divide-and-conquer, and backtracking.
